chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: Back with Illinois Jacquet, and bringing in drummer Dude Brown
summary: Jacquet's band is stuck for a drummer in Providence, and Malachi recommends his boyhood friend George 'Dude' Brown.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: So after Louis broke the band up, this was the first of the year, January, I was in New York, and Illinois Jacquet approached me again about working with him. This is 1951. And it turned out to be a lucky thing, because I went right from Louis' band to Illinois' band. Illinois had most of the same musicians. I think J.J. might have left then. It seems to me he had a fellow from Dayton, Ohio, who later went with Duke Ellington's band, and I can't remember his name right now -- but a very fine trombone player and a wonderful guy. But I guess, not having seen him for so long... His name is right on the tip of my tongue, but I can't remember.
Anyway, I think that the trombone player was different, and by this time Leo Parker had left and we had another baritone saxophone player -- and I don't remember exactly who

No, it wasn't Cecil Payne. Anyway, Jo Jones had been working with Illinois, and Jo left for some reason, and I think Shadow Wilson was supposed to have come back with the band. As a matter of fact, I think Shadow did come back and worked a week or so with him. Then we went to Providence, Rhode Island, and it seems as if, at the time we left New York, Shadow couldn't be found anywhere, and we had to leave without him. In the meantime, Illinois is frantic to have a drummer, and he asked me about a drummer. So I told him I knew this fellow in Washington, D.C., who I had doubt no that he would like. He asked me what his name was, and I told him his name was George Brown -- that's the same Dude Brown that I grew up with.

So we sent and got Dude Brown, and Dude Brown came into Providence. And the rest is history, because I think since then, Illinois has probably used Dude Brown more than any other drummer, here and in Europe and a lot of other places.

Nevertheless, i worked with that band off and on. And at this particular time, Illinois, who had been very hot with the public in '48, when I was with him before, his popularity was beginning to wane somewhat, and work wasn't as consistent as it had been. Nevertheless, during that period, I worked with

him off and on, whenever he had a job. If he had three or four weeks, he would call me, and I would come, and then after that I would come to Washington and play a gig here and there. Somebody would call me to go out for a couple of days or something.
